headline: A night guard saves wartime files from the shredder
text: On 8 January Christoph Meili, a security guard at the Bankgesellschaft in Zurich, found employees shredding old records, among them files of the Nazi era, and handed some to a Jewish organisation; the press reported it on 14 January. Shredding such records violates a law passed in December 1996 to protect evidence on wartime assets. Swiss banks are already under pressure from US politicians and Jewish groups over dormant accounts of Holocaust victims.
imageCaption: Christoph Meili, the night guard at the Bankgesellschaft who took the files from the shredder room, January 1997

headline: Bad-loan fears hit the major banks
text: By early 1997 it has become obvious that bad loans threaten the viability of some of Japan's major banks. Nippon Credit Bank, one of the three long-term credit banks alongside IBJ, has been struggling to raise funds since the start of the year. IBJ shares fell 27% in January.
imageCaption: The head office of Hokkaido Takushoku Bank in Sapporo, one of Japan's big city banks

headline: Wal-Mart joins the Dow Jones Industrial Average
text: On 17 March Wal-Mart replaced Woolworth in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, alongside Hewlett-Packard, Johnson & Johnson and Travelers, which replaced Westinghouse, Texaco and Bethlehem Steel. Wal-Mart's yearly sales have passed 100 billion dollars.
imageCredit: Mike Kalasnik from Fort Mill, USA

headline: Office 97 drives a 45% jump in sales
text: Microsoft's revenue for the quarter to March was 3.21 billion dollars, 45% more than a year earlier, driven by the new Office 97. More than three quarters of new PCs now come with Windows 95, and sales of Windows NT for business servers are growing fastest. Earlier in April Microsoft agreed to buy WebTV Networks for about 425 million dollars.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/0000891020-97-000879.txt (Microsoft 10-Q for the quarter to 31 March 1997, read 2026-10-03); https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/shows/history/history-of-microsoft-1997 (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: The Windows 95 and Microsoft Plus! installation CD

headline: Amazon.com, the online bookstore, goes public
text: Amazon.com of Seattle sold 3 million shares on the Nasdaq on May 15 at $18 each. The company, which opened as 'Earth's Biggest Bookstore' on the World Wide Web in July 1995, had sales of $15.7 million in 1996, up from $511,000, and a net loss of $5.8 million. Founder Jeff Bezos says it will keep spending to grow; Barnes & Noble sued it days before the listing over its claim to be the world's largest bookstore.
imageCaption: Jeff Bezos among stacks of books in Amazon's Seattle warehouse, January 1997, four months before the listing

headline: Switch sales lift Cisco after a spring scare
text: Cisco's sales in the quarter to late April rose 52% to $1.65 billion from $1.09 billion a year earlier, driven by its Catalyst 5000 switches and its 2500, 4700 and 7500 router families. The shares had fallen by about a third in February and March.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000858877/000089161897002545/0000891618-97-002545.txt (10-Q for the quarter to April 27, 1997, read 2026-10-03)
imageCredit: Cisco Systems (Center for Cisco Heritage archive, Computer History Museum)

headline: Iranians elect the reformer Khatami by a landslide
text: Mohammad Khatami, a reformist cleric, won Iran's presidential election on 23 May with 69 percent of the vote, against 25 percent for the conservative Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri. Turnout was about 80 percent, up from 50 percent last time; women and young voters carried him, in a country where more than half the people are under 25 and the voting age is 15. He promises a more open society at home, with fewer restrictions on dress and on satellite television, and better relations abroad. The Guardian Council had barred 234 hopefuls, leaving four candidates.

headline: Speculators attack the Thai baht
text: Thailand's economy has grown by more than 9% a year on average since 1985, and its neighbours have boomed too: the 'tigers' South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong, and the younger 'tiger cubs' Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines. Much of the boom was financed with foreign loans, often short-term and in dollars, and a good part went into property; the baht has been pegged at about 25 to the dollar, so borrowers felt safe. On 14 and 15 May the baht was hit by massive speculative attacks, as traders bet that Thailand, which spends far more abroad than it earns, cannot hold the peg.

headline: Tobacco industry offers a 368.5 billion dollar national settlement
text: On 20 June state attorneys general and the big tobacco companies announced the outline of a national settlement: the companies would pay 368.5 billion dollars over 25 years, accept possible regulation by the Food and Drug Administration and limits on marketing, and in return get protection from class actions. It needs the approval of Congress.
imageCaption: A Marlboro Man billboard in downtown Atlanta, mid-1990s; the proposed settlement would end such outdoor advertising
imageCredit: In Pictures Ltd./Corbis via Getty Images

headline: Hong Kong returns to China
text: Britain handed Hong Kong back to China at a ceremony in the new wing of the city's convention centre on the night of 30 June; Tung Chee-hwa took office on 1 July as head of the new Special Administrative Region. With about 6.5 million people, Hong Kong was Britain's last major colony. Under the agreement Margaret Thatcher and China's premier Zhao Ziyang signed in 1984, its capitalist system and way of life are to stay unchanged for 50 years: 'one country, two systems'.

headline: Thailand lets the baht go
text: On 2 July Thailand gave up its peg of about 25 baht to the dollar and let the currency float, two days after Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh had said he would not devalue; it lacked the foreign reserves needed to defend it. The dollar cost on average about 30 baht in July. Companies that borrowed in dollars now owe far more in baht. Within days speculators turned on Malaysia's ringgit.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Asian_financial_crisis (read 2026-10-04); https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/asian-financial-crisis (read 2026-10-04); FRED series EXTHUS, monthly baht per dollar, https://fred.stlouisfed.org/data/EXTHUS.txt (read 2026-10-04)

headline: Amazon's sales jump twelvefold
text: Amazon's sales in the quarter to June were $27.9 million, against $2.2 million a year earlier, as more customers bought and existing customers came back. The company is still losing money, spending heavily on marketing.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/0000891020-97-001148.txt (10-Q for the quarter to June 30, 1997, read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Jeff Bezos, founder and chief executive of Amazon.com, in the company's Seattle warehouse, 1997
imageCredit: Photograph by Paul Souders — Getty Images

headline: Asian currency crisis hits Coca-Cola and other multinationals
text: Since Thailand let its currency fall in July, the crisis has spread through Southeast Asia, and the dollar has jumped against Asian currencies. On 11 August the IMF unveiled a rescue package of more than $17 billion for Thailand. Shares of multinationals like Coca-Cola, Gillette, General Electric and McDonald's fell in August on worries that slower growth in Asia and the strong dollar will eat into their earnings. Coca-Cola shares lost about 17% in the month.

headline: Jobs makes peace with Microsoft
text: Gil Amelio was pushed out as chief executive on 9 July, and Steve Jobs is now interim chief executive. At the Macworld show on 6 August Jobs announced that Microsoft will invest 150 million dollars in Apple, keep making Office for the Mac for five years and settle the long patent dispute. Apple is worth only about 2.5 billion dollars.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Apple_Inc. (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/320193/0000320193-97-000012.txt (Apple 8-K with press release of 9 July 1997) (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Amelio (read 2026-10-03)
imageCaption: Bill Gates appears on the giant screen above Steve Jobs at Macworld Boston as the Microsoft investment in Apple is announced, 6 August 1997

headline: Hong Kong crash drags down Wall Street
text: Hong Kong's Hang Seng index fell 23% between 20 and 23 October as speculators attacked the Hong Kong dollar's peg. On 27 October the Dow Jones fell 554 points, or 7.2%, and trading was halted early; it regained 337 points the next day. Indonesia agreed a $23 billion rescue led by the IMF on 31 October.
imageCaption: A floor trader at the Hong Kong stock exchange the day after the crash, as the Hang Seng rebounds, 29 October 1997
imageCredit: Photo by David Wong/South China Morning Post via Getty Images

headline: The new A-Class tips over in the 'elk test'
text: On 21 October the new Mercedes A-Class, the brand's first small car, rolled onto its side and roof in a swerving test by the Swedish magazine Teknikens Värld. Daimler-Benz responded that it will fit its electronic stability programme ESP to every A-Class as standard, so far a feature of luxury cars. At the end of the month the Asian financial crisis caused a crash on stock markets worldwide.
imageCaption: A Mercedes A-Class weaving through the cones of the elk test, the swerve that tipped the car over in Sweden in October 1997

headline: Yamaichi and Hokkaido Takushoku collapse
text: Major financial firms failed almost weekly in November: Sanyo Securities on 3 November, Hokkaido Takushoku Bank, and on 24 November Yamaichi Securities, one of Japan's four largest brokers. Japanese banks' bad debts are estimated at 264 to 304 billion dollars. Since the outcry over the 685 billion yen of taxpayers' money used in 1996 to wind up the jusen, the failed housing lenders, public money for banks has been almost taboo in Tokyo.
imageCaption: Kayabacho Tower in Tokyo, the headquarters of Yamaichi Securities

headline: WorldCom to take over MCI for $37 billion
text: WorldCom agreed to buy MCI Communications, the second-largest U.S. long-distance company and more than three times WorldCom's size, for about $37 billion in stock, the largest takeover in history. MCI had been about to merge with British Telecom.
imageCaption: Bernard Ebbers, chief executive of WorldCom

headline: Bankgesellschaft and Bankverein to merge into UBS
text: On 8 December the Bankgesellschaft and the Bankverein announced an all-stock 'merger of equals' under the name UBS. Bankgesellschaft shareholders get about 60% of the new bank. 13,000 jobs are to go, more than half in Switzerland; the bank targets 10-11 billion francs of profit within four years and would be the world's largest manager of private wealth, with more than 1,000 billion francs of client assets. The Bankverein's Marcel Ospel becomes chief executive, the Bankgesellschaft's Mathis Cabiallavetta chairman. The Bankgesellschaft has recently suffered losses on equity derivatives.
imageCaption: Marcel Ospel of the Bankverein (left) and Mathis Cabiallavetta of the Bankgesellschaft on their way to the press conference announcing the merger, Zurich, 8 December 1997

headline: South Korea needs the IMF
text: On 3 December South Korea agreed a three-year rescue with the International Monetary Fund, part of a package of $58.4 billion. Korean banks and companies owe an estimated $100 billion in short-term foreign debt, and foreign lenders pulled back after Hong Kong's crash in October. The won lost about 20% against the dollar by the end of November and shares fell by some 30% to a ten-year low. Big conglomerates have been failing since the Hanbo group went bankrupt early in the year, and Kia Motors needed emergency loans in July.
